parts.text: Hallway Track. Find the right talk, whoever you are.
Built at the Cloud Native Hackathon in Salt Lake City, by Dennis Stewart, team Denn.
Conferences are hard to navigate, and harder if you need captions, a step-free room, or a quiet seat.
Hallway Track lets you describe what you want to learn in your own words, then filters talks by what you need to take part.
Search by meaning, set your needs once, and plan your day.
Here is how it works.
The browser loads a plain HTML page and calls a Swift server built on SwiftNIO.
The server asks Elasticsearch to find talks by keyword and by meaning, using Jina embeddings and a Jina reranker.
Every request sends traces and metrics to Dash0, and the whole app runs on Kubernetes, where Radar can watch it.
One container serves both the page and the API.
A Dockerfile builds it, Kubernetes runs it with health probes and an autoscaler, and Argo CD deploys each push.
Gitar reviews the pull requests, and a continuous integration job runs the relevance tests.
The manifests are written. Launching them on a cluster is the part still being verified.
Search is the heart of it.
Elasticsearch combines keyword matching with semantic search, then a Jina reranker puts the best talks first.
Each result says whether it matched your words, your meaning, or both.
Plain phrases like I use a wheelchair become visible filters, such as step-free access, that you can remove at any time.
On top of search, My agenda builds a time-zone-correct schedule and flags clashes, and it can suggest a swap.
Quiet route uses a live room-fill signal to suggest calmer, step-free, captioned rooms.
Access filters cover captions, sign language, step-free rooms, quiet rooms, and slides with alt text.
A health strip shows how fast each search was, with a trace ID you can copy.
To use it, type what you want to learn. Press slash to jump to the search box.
Pick your needs once, and they apply to every search.
Add talks to My agenda, then check the health strip to see how the app is doing.
Accessibility is built in, not added later.
Every control works from the keyboard with a visible focus ring, and results are announced to screen readers.
State never relies on colour alone, and the page respects reduced motion and forced colours.
There is a dyslexia-friendly font option and a fallback that works without JavaScript.
Manual checks in Safari and with VoiceOver are the last step.
The demo story is Keynote Rush.
A load test simulates a hundred and seventy attendees opening their agenda at once, right after the keynote.
Dash0 shows the slowdown, and Agent0 points to the cause.
Radar watches the cluster respond, and a Gitar-reviewed pull request ships the fix.
What is built: the Swift server, the page, My agenda, room fill, the relevance tests, and the deploy files.
Still being verified: the cluster launch, the Elasticsearch relevance numbers, and browser monitoring in Dash0.
Thank you. This is Hallway Track, by Dennis Stewart, team Denn.
